'''Melissa Marie Hines''' (born November 27, 1951)<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kBRbAAAAYAAJ |title=The 1973 Nassau Herald |date=1973 |pages=198 |language=en |via=[[Google Books]]}}</ref> is an American neuroscientist, [[psychobiologist]], and professor at the [[University of Cambridge]]. She studies the development of gender, with particular focus on how the interaction of prenatal and postnatal experience shape brain development and behavior.

== Early life and education ==
Melissa Marie Hines was born on November 27, 1951, in [[Moline, Illinois]].<ref name=":0" /> Her parents were Janice ([[née]] Sersig) and William Joseph Hines.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=January 3, 2007 |title=Janice Hines Obituary (2007) Washington, DC |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/washingtonpost/name/janice-hines-obituary?id=5580670 |access-date=2025-05-12 |website=Legacy.com |publisher=[[The Washington Post]]}}</ref> She graduated from [[Georgetown Visitation Preparatory School]] in Washington, D.C.<ref name=":0" />

Hines received a [[bachelor's degree]] in [[psychology]] from [[Princeton University]].<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date= 23 November 2014|title=Professor of Psychology, Melissa Hines |url=https://www.psychol.cam.ac.uk/about-us/athena-swan/celebration-of-women/prof-melissa-hines |access-date=2018-02-03 |website=Department of Psychology, University of Cambridge |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Walter |first=Natasha |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SpMzAgAAQBAJ&pg=PT125 |title=Living Dolls: The Return of Sexism |date=2011-05-26 |publisher=Little, Brown Book Group |isbn=978-0-7481-3206-5 |pages=125 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Fine |first=Cordelia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JbdkAgAAQBAJ&pg=PT36 |title=Delusions of Gender: The Real Science Behind Sex Differences |date=2005-02-01 |publisher=Icon Books Ltd |isbn=978-1-84831-396-5 |pages=36 |language=en}}</ref> She was in the first group of women enrolled as undergraduates,<ref name=":1" /> which could have inspired an interest in gender.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://paw.princeton.edu/article/when-women-came-princeton|title=When Women Came to Princeton|date=2016-10-18|work=Princeton Alumni Weekly|access-date=2018-02-03|language=en}}</ref> She received a [[PhD]] in 1981 in psychology from the [[University of California, Los Angeles]]. The focus of her thesis was the gender-related behaviour of women whose mothers had taken the synthetic [[oestrogen]] [[diethylstilbestrol]] during pregnancy.<ref name="Churchill College">{{Cite web |title=People – Professor Melissa Hines |url=https://www.chu.cam.ac.uk/people/view/melissa-hines/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151017031247/https://www.chu.cam.ac.uk/people/view/melissa-hines/ |archive-date=October 17, 2015 |access-date=2018-02-03 |website=Churchill College {{Primary source inline|date=May 2025}}}}</ref>

== Research ==
Hines completed a [[postdoctoral fellowship]] in [[neuroendocrinology]] and [[neuroscience]] at the [[University of California, Los Angeles|UCLA]] Brain Research Institute.<ref name="GDRC">{{Cite web |last= |first= |date= |title=People — Gender Development Research Centre |url=https://www.gdrc.psychol.cam.ac.uk/people |access-date=2018-02-03 |website=www.gdrc.psychol.cam.ac.uk {{Primary source inline|date=May 2025}} |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=March 7, 1983 |title=Differences in male and female brains |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-modesto-bee-differences-in-male-and/172202226/ |access-date=2025-05-12 |work=[[The Modesto Bee]] |pages=13}}</ref> She investigated hormonal influences on brain development in rodents there and at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison|University of Wisconsin, Madison]] where she was a visiting scientist.<ref name="Hines-2004">{{Cite book |last=Melissa. |first=Hines |title=Brain gender |date=2004 |publisher=Oxford University Press {{Primary source inline|date=May 2025}} |isbn=9780195188363 |location=Oxford |oclc=51804960}}</ref> She received the [[Shepherd Ivory Franz|Shephard Ivory Franz]] Award for Distinguished Teaching at [[University of California, Los Angeles|UCLA]].<ref name="Elsevier/Academic Press-2009">{{Cite book|title=Hormones, brain, and behavior|date=2009|publisher=Elsevier/Academic Press|others=Pfaff, Donald W., 1939-, Elsevier Science (Firm)|isbn=978-0080887838|edition= 2nd electronic|location=Amsterdam|oclc=449286151}}</ref> After her postdoctoral fellowship, she was appointed as an assistant and then associate professor at UCLA. During her time at UCLA she trained and was licensed as a clinical psychologist.<ref name="Hines-2004" />

Hines moved to the UK and joined City University as a professor of psychology in 1996.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.staff.city.ac.uk/m.hines/|title=Home Page|website=www.staff.city.ac.uk {{Primary source inline|date=May 2025}}|access-date=2018-02-03}}</ref> She is a chartered counseling psychologist in the UK ([[British Psychological Society]]).<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date= |title=Good practice guidelines for the assessment and treatment of adults with gender dysphoria |url=http://www.gires.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2014/08/CR181_Nov15.pdf |access-date=2018-02-03 |website=Gender Identity Research & Education Society {{Primary source inline|date=May 2025}}}}</ref> In 2006 she joined the University of Cambridge, and [[Churchill College, Cambridge]].<ref name="Churchill College" /> She is director of the [[University of Cambridge]]s's Gender Development Research Centre.<ref name="GDRC" />

Her research focuses on the causes and consequences of sex/gender differences in human brain and behaviour.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Cahill|first=Larry|title=His Brain, Her Brain|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/his-brain-her-brain-2012-10-23/|journal=Scientific American|language=en|volume=21|issue=2s|pages=4–11|doi=10.1038/scientificamericanbrain0512-4|year=2012|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last=poppy sebag-montefiore|title=The Brain and the Mind - Discussion 5 of 6: The Gendered Brain|date=2013-08-09|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ydl3VaaqMsY|accessdate=2018-02-03}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Aleshire |first=Peter |date=1989-07-22 |title=Exploring boy-girl differences |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/oakland-tribune-exploring-boy-girl-diffe/172202308/ |access-date=2025-05-12 |work=[[Oakland Tribune]] |pages=8 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> Based on findings that male and female vervet monkeys show toy preferences that resemble those seen in children, Hines and Alexander suggested that "sex differences in toy preferences can arise independent of the social and cognitive mechanisms thought by many to be the primary influences on toy preferences".<ref name="Hines 478–479">{{Cite journal |last1=Hines |first1=Melissa |last2=Alexander |first2=Gerianne M. |year=2008 |title=Monkeys, girls, boys and toys: A confirmation |journal=Hormones and Behavior |volume=54 |issue=3 |pages=478–479 |doi=10.1016/j.yhbeh.2008.05.012 |pmc=2643016 |pmid=18599056 |via={{Primary source inline|date=May 2025}}}}</ref> Other research indicates that girls with high levels of testosterone are less interested in dolls, and more interested in toy vehicles, than are other girls.<ref name="Hines 478–479"/><ref>{{Citation|last=Clare Bailey|title=Clare Rayner BBC Breakfast: Why is pink the colour of choice for girls?|date=2011-05-09|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yMwb8FNlTt8|accessdate=2018-02-03}}</ref> She has appeared on a discussion panel with autism researcher Simon Baron Cohen, who also is interested in hormonal influences on human gender development.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.thebrainandthemind.co.uk/The_Talks/Talk5/|title=The Brain and the Mind|last=Ltd.|first=Thomas Dale of D Taled Designs|website=www.thebrainandthemind.co.uk|access-date=2018-02-03}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2014-11-29 |title=Have you a male or a female brain? |url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/lifestyle/healthandlife/relationships/have-you-a-male-or-a-female-brain-299884.html |access-date=2018-02-03 |work=The Irish Examiner}}</ref> Their results have, however, sometimes differed from one another's, with Hines' results showing an influence just for girls but Baron Cohen's showing an influence just for boys or for boys and girls taken together, and for some measures no difference for either sex.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.slate.com/articles/double_x/doublex/2010/10/the_last_word_on_fetal_t.html|title=The Last Word on Fetal T|last=Schaffer|first=Amanda|date=2010-10-21|work=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]|access-date=2018-02-03|language=en-US|issn=1091-2339}}</ref>

== Public engagement ==
Hines was the President of the [[International Academy of Sex Research]].<ref name="Elsevier/Academic Press-2009" /> She is the author of ''[[Brain Gender]]'', published in 2005 by [[Oxford University Press]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bailey |first=Susan E. |date=October 2005 |title=Brain Gender |url=https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/full/10.1176/appi.ps.56.10.1325 |journal=[[Psychiatric Services]] |volume=56 |issue=10 |pages=1325 |doi=10.1176/appi.ps.56.10.1325 |issn=1075-2730|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Tenenbaum-2006">{{Cite journal |last1=Tenenbaum |first1=Harriet R. |last2=Hill |first2=Darryl B. |date=November 2006 |title=Book Review: Brain Gender |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0959353506068789 |journal=[[Feminism & Psychology]] |language=en |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=495–501 |doi=10.1177/0959353506068789 |issn=0959-3535|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

She spoke at the [[Lucy Cavendish College, Cambridge]] "Women's Word" festival in 2011.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.cam.ac.uk/research/news/is-there-any-such-thing-as-the-female-brain|title=Is there any such thing as the female brain?|date=2011-06-22|work=University of Cambridge |access-date=2018-02-03|language=en}}</ref> In 2013 she appeared on BBC Radio 4 discussing the spat between [[Suzanne Moore]] and transgender rights activists.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b01rbrtd|title=Who Decides if I'm a Woman?, Analysis - BBC Radio 4|website=BBC|language=en-GB|access-date=2018-02-03}}</ref> In 2014 she was an invited speaker at the [[Cambridge Science Festival]]. She is a writer for [[The Conversation (website)|The Conversation]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Hines |first=Melissa |title=There's no good reason to push pink toys on girls |url=https://theconversation.com/theres-no-good-reason-to-push-pink-toys-on-girls-15830 |access-date=2018-02-03 |work=The Conversation {{Primary source inline|date=May 2025}} |language=en}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Her partner starting in 1986, was [[Richard Green (sexologist)|Richard Green]] (1936–2019), a noted psychiatrist and sexologist; they married in 1994 and were divorced in 2014.<ref name="Carey-2019">{{Cite news |last=Carey |first=Benedict |date=2019-04-17 |title=Dr. Richard Green, 82, Dies; Challenged Psychiatry's View of Homosexuality |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/04/17/obituaries/dr-richard-green-dead.html |access-date=2020-09-18 |work=[[The New York Times]] |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref name=TheTimes-2019>{{Cite web |date=19 July 2019 |title=Richard Green obituary |url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/richard-green-obituary-xg9gdgzqk |access-date=2025-05-12 |website=[[The Times]] |language=en}}</ref> Together they had one son.<ref name="Carey-2019" /><ref name=TheTimes-2019 />
